source.title: When unlearning is free: leveraging low influence points to reduce computational costs
source.authors: Anat Kleiman; Robert Fisher; Ben Deaner; Udi Wieder

record.file_problem: The supplied text appears to contain the full paper; no material truncation or garbling noted.
record.tranche_reason: Applies influence-based point removal in image and language settings and reports retrained accuracy on omitted examples; it does not test the claim versions’ specific interventions or measures.
record.gate_note: The study measures how well models retrained without low-influence examples classify those omitted examples, and compares with random removals. This bears on generalization but does not directly test any listed version. Cited prior results and figure-only outcomes are not separately cataloged here.
record.test_reason: Table 22 tests V5 in a new setting: retain-set training during CIFAR-10 class-wise unlearning. With 20 epochs fixed, batch size 500 gives 70.5% test accuracy versus 75.1% at 128 and 75.0% at 256. The influence-removal experiments do not test V8: they remove low-influence examples and evaluate accuracy on those examples, rather than removing the most memorized examples and measuring independent test accuracy.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases the authors' main conclusion: influence-based filtering identifies examples that remain predictable without inclusion in retraining, and reducing forget and retain sets can cut unlearning runtime by up to approximately 50% while preserving comparable measured utility and privacy outcomes. These are empirical comparisons, not a demonstrated general privacy guarantee.
record.recipe_differences: Influence-based point selection and retraining or unlearning; not a test of the listed claim versions’ original methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The study says influence rankings can depend on training order and specific training conditions; CIFAR-100 tolerates fewer removals before performance degradation than CIFAR-10.

fits_no_version.finding: After low-influence removal, omitted-point accuracy exceeds that of separately selected random-removal sets: 97.7–99.2% versus 90.9–92.3% for forget-set removals, and 95.5–99.0% versus 87.1–90.6% for the recorded retain-set removals.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Influence filtering identifies subsets that remain readily predictable when omitted from retraining. These comparisons evaluate different selected subsets and do not establish the effect of removing highly memorized examples on independent test accuracy.

record.problems: The selected points are defined by influence approximations, and the text notes individual low influence does not guarantee low collective influence. Table 15 gives no uncertainty estimates. The reported omitted-point accuracy is not the claim versions’ test-error measure.
record.rows_left_out: Other retrained-accuracy, unlearning accuracy, runtime, membership-inference, and competition-metric results appear in Figures 4.1–5.3, Tables 1–14, and Tables 16–24. They concern unlearning quality, runtime, or task-specific utility rather than a listed claim version; not extracted as additional rows.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and chance-level random-label test accuracy alongside natural-label generalization under the same recipe.
Width sweeps beyond zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer comparisons under specified tuning budgets.

Initial training from scratch, language models, longer-training rescue, learning-rate scaling and warmup, and normalization or regularization adaptations. The batch-size ablation concerns retain-set training during unlearning.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its ranking of generalization gaps.
Removing the most memorized examples versus equally many random examples and comparing independent test accuracy after retraining.

missing.what: Extract the fixed-20-epoch batch-size ablation as V5 rows: batch sizes 64, 128, 256 and 500 yield test accuracies 74.2%, 75.1%, 75.0% and 70.5%, respectively; retain accuracies are 89.9%, 92.2%, 90.5% and 82.2%. Although rows_left_out mentions Table 22, it incorrectly dismisses its relevance to every version.
missing.locator: Appendix K.3, Table 22; the table specifies Class 0, while the preceding prose says Class 1.

record.verdict_notes: Table 15's numerical values are correctly transcribed. Its baseline accuracies concern the original forget or retain sets, whereas subsequent accuracies concern selected omitted subsets; they are not matched-subset before/after measurements. No verdict follows from these rows. The study is not an original source for V5.

Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizer generalization comparisons.

Dropout interventions and their effects on held-out error.

relationships.condition: Rank 1 CIFAR-10 class-wise unlearning, retain-set training for 20 epochs; batch size 500 versus 128 or 256.
relationships.reason: Based on Table 22 text, since no extracted row captures this comparison: test accuracy falls from 75.1% at batch 128 and 75.0% at 256 to 70.5% at 500. Retain accuracy also falls, from 92.2% and 90.5% to 82.2%, so the result does not isolate a larger train–test gap.
relationships.display_finding: The study reports lower test accuracy and lower retain accuracy (accuracy on data the model is meant to retain) at the largest batch. These comparisons remain unverified and do not establish that the gap between training and test performance widened.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
